content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to allow its own experts to review the forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Here are the details.

A little background

Earlier this July, Apple filed a lawsuit against a former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of misappropriating trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves a former Apple employee who allegedly took confidential information when leaving the company. Apple also accuses former employee Chang Liu of coaching another Apple employee on what materials to review before the latter's interview with the company, while Tang Tan instructed Apple job candidates to bring hardware components and other materials to the interview venue.

Previously, Apple stated that preliminary forensic examination showed a MacBook used by Liu after leaving the company had been used during his time at OpenAI to run a simulation of an Apple confidential circuit schematic. Apple also pointed out that the MacBook showed Liu had used a Mac mini, which the company has since requested access to as part of the case.

OpenAI subsequently pushed back against Apple's allegations, claiming the incident was an "Apple-made mess," because the company's offboarding procedures and security measures were alleged to be so lax that employees could more easily inadvertently retain access to confidential information after leaving.

One of the major points of contention in the case is Apple's motion to expedite discovery, which OpenAI opposes. Another point of contention is Apple's request for an injunction to restrict OpenAI from using its alleged trade secrets during the litigation, which could affect hardware development currently underway at OpenAI.

Apple argues that precisely because OpenAI is still developing hardware products, expedited discovery is necessary, as the alleged use of Apple's trade secrets could further entangle with the relevant work, becoming increasingly difficult to reverse.

OpenAI countered that Apple has not demonstrated why a separate expedited discovery process is needed, and claimed Apple's requests are overly broad.

With the parties at an impasse, the court ordered both sides to submit a joint document outlining their respective positions on expedited discovery. That document was filed last Friday and has been made public.

Apple seeks access to forensic images and R&D materials

In the joint document, Apple asked the court to allow its own forensic experts to review the underlying forensic images relied upon by the defendants' experts — images used to analyze Liu's devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple's confidential information after leaving the company.

Apple stated that one of its forensic experts had identified what they described as "significant gaps" in the defendants' experts' analysis, and believes its experts need direct access to the materials to determine whether there are other issues with the defendants' forensic analysis.

Apple's statement reads:

Apple's forensic expert has found several significant gaps in the analysis conducted by the defendants' experts, including: (1) failure to locate on Mr. Liu's Mac mini files clearly shown to have been used and stored on the device; (2) incorrectly equating files of zero bytes or empty kMDItemLastUsedDate fields on the Mac mini with those files never having been accessed. … Allowing Apple's experts direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other mistakes the defendants' experts may have made.

OpenAI believes Apple's experts should not be granted unrestricted access to the forensic images, and instead proposes that a neutral forensic expert handle the relevant materials under a mutually agreed-upon protocol.

Apple argues this would put it at a disadvantage, because the defendants' own forensic experts have already had direct access to the same materials.

Beyond the forensic materials, Apple is also seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including work on metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI had previously argued that its metal finishing technology was developed independently and did not use Apple's confidential information; it also claimed that the simulations Liu ran using Apple confidential files have nothing to do with its upcoming products.

Apple is now requesting the underlying development documentation to verify OpenAI's claims, but OpenAI says this is merely an attempt to "spy on a competitor."

The joint document also addresses several other points of contention, including:

  • Apple is further seeking forensic images of devices used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng, and another OpenAI employee — devices that currently or previously contained what Apple has defined as "Apple-derived materials";
  • Records related to Liu's use of AI tools. The defendants previously stated that the forensic investigation found no evidence of him using Apple confidential files on platforms such as ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Interview-related documents from OpenAI's consumer hardware division, including materials actually used during the interview process at that division, as well as communications with departing Apple employees;
  • OpenAI stated that Apple's written discovery requests could involve as many as 400 current OpenAI employees who previously worked at Apple.

Apple is also seeking the complete LINE conversation records between Liu and Peng, which include conversations in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about his work at Apple after Liu had left the company.

The defendants have already submitted excerpts of some of these conversations as part of their argument against Apple's motion for an injunction, but Apple believes it should be permitted to review the full conversations rather than only the messages the defendants chose to submit.
